title: Your video did not lose to the algorithm. It lost at hello.
markdown:
# Your video did not lose to the algorithm. It lost at hello.

At 9:14 p.m., you watch your edit one more time before posting. The color looks right. The cut at eight seconds is clean. You hit publish, then look at the retention graph the next morning. It drops before you have even said what the video is about.

That drop is usually not a verdict on the whole video. It is a problem with the opening promise. A stranger scrolling past needs to know, fast, why this clip is worth interrupting their thumb for.

This article is for the creator who has useful things to say but keeps losing viewers before the second sentence. By the end, you will have a repeatable way to write openings that give a viewer a reason to stay, plus a simple way to test them.

## Treat the first line as a promise

The beginning of a short video has one job: make a specific promise that the next few seconds will pay off. "Hey guys, today I want to talk about..." spends that tiny window on housekeeping. So does a broad label like "Three tips for better content." The viewer can find thousands of videos that sound like that.

Start with the friction your viewer already feels, a result they want, or a belief they may be ready to question. Then make the rest of the video answer that opening line.

For example, a fitness coach talking to beginners could begin with:

"Stop trying to work out every day in week one."

That is not a complete argument. It does not need to be. It gives the viewer a disagreement to resolve. The next sentence has a clear task: explain why the daily plan makes beginners quit and what to do instead.

The useful test is blunt: if you removed the rest of the video, would the first line make a person want the next line? If it only names the topic, rewrite it.

## Write five openings before choosing one

Most weak hooks are not terrible. They are simply the first thought the creator wrote down. That is a poor reason to film it.

Take one video idea and make several versions that approach it from different angles. Here is a topic: a small coffee shop wants to show why its cold brew tastes less bitter.

- Curiosity: "Why does your cold brew taste bitter after day two?"
- Contrarian: "Ice is probably ruining your cold brew."
- Stakes: "If you pour cold brew like this, you are wasting the good part."
- Result: "This one change made our cold brew taste less sharp."
- Callout: "Coffee people who hate bitter cold brew, try this first."

Each line gives the same video a different doorway. The curiosity version asks a question. The contrarian version pushes against a familiar habit. The result version works best only if the video can show the change quickly. None needs a made-up statistic or a grand claim.

Keep spoken hooks short enough to say without racing. Around a dozen words is a useful ceiling. Write the on-screen text separately, too. A viewer may read before they hear you, or watch with sound off. The text should reinforce the spoken line, not repeat a long sentence in smaller type.

## Match the hook to the proof you can show

A hook can get a click and still damage the video if the body cannot deliver on it. "This changes everything" asks for a payoff almost nobody can prove in 30 seconds. A narrower promise earns more trust.

Before filming, write two lines under every hook:

- What will the viewer see in the first ten seconds that proves this was worth stopping for?
- What should they do after watching?

For the cold-brew example, the proof could be a side-by-side pour, a quick explanation of dilution, and one instruction to try at home. If the proof is only "listen while I explain," choose a hook that promises an explanation, not a dramatic result.

This also prevents a common trap: copying a hook that worked for someone else's audience. A finance creator can open with a tax deadline. A recipe creator cannot borrow that urgency and expect it to make sense. The hook has to belong to the subject, the viewer, and the footage you can make.

## Build the rest of the video around the opening

Once you choose a hook, the structure gets simpler. In a 30-second video, try this:

1. First three seconds: say the hook and show the visual that makes it believable.
2. Next seven seconds: name the problem in plain language.
3. Middle: give the demonstration, explanation, or before-and-after.
4. Final seconds: give one next step that fits the video.

The goal is not to stuff every useful fact into one clip. Leave the viewer with one clear idea they can use. A video about bitter cold brew can teach dilution. It does not also need to cover beans, grinders, water chemistry, and every brewing method.

## Test the opening, not your self-worth

When an opening underperforms, keep the lesson small. Do not conclude that you are bad on camera or that the platform has decided against you. Change one part of the opening and make another version.

You might keep the same footage and test a question against a callout. Or keep the spoken line and change the first on-screen text. Watch where viewers leave, then compare videos that address the same audience and topic. One post is a clue, not a ruling.

Write down the hooks that hold attention and the ones that do not. Over time, you will notice what your own viewers respond to: a direct problem, a visible result, a strong opinion, or something else. That record is more useful than a folder of generic prompts.

## When you need a full first pass

Writing five real options, choosing one, and turning it into a shootable script takes more effort than it looks. If you have the topic but need a complete first pass, Hook Lab is built for that narrow job. Give it a topic, product, trend, or niche and it returns distinct first-three-second hooks with spoken lines and on-screen text, a recommended option, a timecoded short-form script, a caption, and a filming tip for TikTok, Reels, or Shorts.

Use the result as raw material, then make it yours. The best hook is not the loudest sentence on the screen. It is the opening your particular viewer believes long enough to hear you out.
